B00.said: Hello. This is Uh-mohg Muddoor. The voice is synthetic; the claims are mine. You open an AI chat and type: help me write a cover letter. It doesn't know who you are, what the job is, or what to avoid. So it has to guess. Tomorrow you'll type that background again, or set it up separately on every site you use.

B01.said: Here it is in one breath. Getting more from AI is not a wording problem. It is a context problem. Fix the background, and you fix the answer. And the more a tool is allowed to do, the more the missing background costs.

B02.said: Here is what Pepper does about it. You type the same rough request. Pepper turns it into a full prompt, using what you've already told it: who the AI should be, the background it can't guess, what to write, the rules, the layout, and what done looks like. It drops that in the box. You press send.

B03.said: Now the argument. Missing context is not one bug with one size. Its cost scales with what the tool may do. A tool that only reads your typing gets you a worse paragraph. A tool that sends for you gets you an answer you never checked. A tool that can act on your account gets you something you cannot undo. Pepper stops at the second rung, on purpose.

B04.said: Here is the part that makes it more than a template. When the prompt needs a fact about you that Pepper does not have, it is not allowed to invent one. Facts may come only from your stored profile, memories and files. Anything else lands in this box, outside the prompt, until you add it yourself. Missing context is shown, not filled.

B05.said: Why not use what already exists? Two of them, read this morning on their own pages. ChatGPT's custom instructions: standing text, applied to every chat, one site, kept on your account. Second, a prompt-library extension with five thousand four hundred templates that somebody else wrote. Both are real, and both are useful. Neither one tells you what it had to guess.

B06.said: So what actually exists. The suite ran this morning, on this machine. Seventy-five unit tests, seventy-five passing, in about six seconds. Twenty browser checks, re-run today, all passing. Twenty-two screenshots that suite produced. And one more number, the one nobody puts in bold: how many live sites any of it has touched.

B07.said: Here is what could sink it, and it is not subtle. Every one of those checks ran against mock pages, and the mocks were built from Pepper's own selectors. So the tests cannot catch a wrong selector. They are made of it. The fix is a measurement: twenty inserts per live site, against the project's own bar of ninety-nine percent, re-run every Chrome release.

B08.said: And the one thing it will never do. Pepper will not press send. That is not a missing feature; it is the boundary. It asks for two browser permissions. It reads the prompt box, not the page. The moment a tool sends for you, it needs permission to act, and acting on context nobody checked is where the damage starts.

B09.said: Now the part a pitch usually skips. Point the same question at my own claim. What would have to be true for 'Pepper works' to be wrong? Three conditions, and not one of them has been tested. The selectors could be stale. A real model might ignore the six-part contract; every model in those tests was a fake. And nobody but me has ever opened it.

B10.said: So why this one? Half is showing off, and I will say which. I designed Pepper and directed the build; Claude wrote the code, and the tests went green. The other half is new: running a check that can come back bad, and publishing the number anyway. Anyone opening this repository should run the tests in a minute, then find that column.

B11.said: So, the verdict, in two lists. Exists today: the extension, seventy-five passing tests, twenty-two screenshots, a protocol with every result cell blank, and a draft privacy notice. Will exist: that protocol run on five live sites, a measured insert rate for each, a failure analysis, and a check that fails loudly when a site moves its box. Nothing in the second list has happened yet.

B12.said: Your turn, and here is the prompt. Take the last tool you shipped. List every claim its README makes. Beside each one, write the exact test that supports it, and where there is none, write: nobody has checked this. Then count the second column. That count separates what you know from what you have been saying. Run it on your own repository. The number is usually worse than you expect.
